title: Privacy and terms
heading: Privacy and *terms*
lede: The short, plain-English version of how this site works and what we do with anything you send us.
seoDescription: How Acacia Climbing Coalition handles your information, and the terms for using this site.

sections.footnote: Acacia Climbing Coalition · ABN 38 237 542 815 · Questions? hello@acaciaclimbing.org

children.text: This site is run by Cooper Flick, trading as Acacia Climbing Coalition (ABN 38 237 542 815), based in Queensland, Australia.

We don't have accounts or a newsletter on this site. If you use the sign-up form or email us, we receive your name, email address and whatever you choose to tell us. If the form is delivered by a form service, that service only passes it on to us.
Our host, Cloudflare, keeps basic technical logs (like IP addresses) to keep the site running and secure.
We only use what you send us to reply to you, coordinate volunteering, and follow up crag reports. We don't sell or share your details, and we'll delete them if you ask.
We handle personal information in line with the Australian Privacy Principles. Email hello@acaciaclimbing.org with any questions or requests.
Access status and crag details here are general information, not permission to climb. Access can change, so always check signage, local rules and any closures before you visit.
Climbing is risky. You're responsible for your own safety and for respecting the land, other users and Traditional Owners.
You're welcome to share and link to anything here with credit to Acacia Climbing Coalition. Detailed guidebook information lives on KAYA under their terms.

heading: Climbers, for the long *haul*
lede: Acacia Climbing Coalition is a small, volunteer-run crew working to get outdoor climbing recognised and looked after across Australia. We're starting in South East Queensland, and building it in the open.

children.text: Most councils in Australia don't have a way to formally recognise outdoor climbing. That leaves crags with unclear access, no stairs or signs, and nobody speaking for climbers when decisions get made.
At the same time, more people than ever are climbing in gyms and wanting to head outside, with very little to tell them where it's okay to go and how to look after it when they get there.

sections.heading: Why we started
sections.quoteBody: A crag that's mapped, written up and known to council is a lot easier to keep open. So that's what we do, one crag at a time, and we share every step along the way.

children.text: Right now there's no modern, actively looked-after guide for Queensland climbing. A lot of what's out there is years old, and some areas have very little public information at all. That's how people end up lost, or bush-bashing new paths that damage the forest around the rock.

We're building that modern guide: made with the community, actively looked after, with clear approach tracks, current access notes, and closures for fires, backburning or roads showing up the day they happen.

sections.heading: Bringing climbing info up to date
sections.quote: "Built to last, like the Access Fund."
sections.quoteBody: In the US, the Access Fund has looked after climbing access alongside land managers for decades. We want Australian climbing set up for the long term in the same way.

sections.label: Where we're up to
sections.heading: Every crag, on one map
sections.body: Tooheys Forest is recognised, White Rock and Plunketts are underway, and Cedar Creek and Passchendaele are just getting started. The map shows where each one is up to.

sections.label: Who's behind it
sections.heading: Started by a local boulderer
sections.body: Acacia was started by Cooper, a South East Queensland boulderer and the bouldering representative for Rock Climbing Queensland (RCQ, formerly ACAQ). He spent a couple of years working towards this before taking it public. Right now it's a small volunteer crew doing the work in spare hours, with a lot of help from local climbers.

children.text: The crags we document sit on the lands of many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, including the Turrbal, Jagera, Yugarapul, Jinibara and Kabi Kabi peoples in South East Queensland. We pay our respects to Elders past and present.
We want consultation with Traditional Owners to be part of how every crag is documented, not an afterthought. We're still building those relationships, and we'll share how that's going as it happens.

title: Guidebooks
heading: Guides that stay *up to date*
lede: Our guidebooks live on KAYA, a climbing app with digital guidebooks. Here's what it is, why we use it, and where the money goes.
seoDescription: Acacia's climbing guidebooks live on KAYA: what KAYA is, why we use it, and where guidebook money goes.

sections.heading: What is KAYA?

children.text: KAYA is a climbing app with digital guidebooks. Every boulder gets a GPS pin, with topo lines, approach notes and beta videos, and you can download a guide to use at the crag without phone reception.
Unlike a printed book, a digital guide can change the day something changes. Authors keep it current, and climbers can report problems as they find them.

sections.quoteBody: A guide that's current, agreed with council and easy to find is the best way we know to keep a crag open and looked after.

cards.title: Closures shown straight away
cards.body: Fire danger, backburning, road closures or a new access rule go into the guide the same day, instead of people relying on years-old information.

cards.title: Everything at the crag
cards.body: Directions, approach tracks, boulder locations and access notes in one place, even with no reception.

cards.title: Agreed before it's public
cards.body: We only publish a guide once the council or land manager is comfortable, and they can see exactly what's out there.

sections.heading: Where the money goes

children.text: Every guidebook on KAYA sends at least 5% of what it earns to the local climbing organisation for that area. In South East Queensland, that's us. Guide authors can also choose to give more of their own share.

We don't keep it. In Australia, signs, stairs and track work are done by contracted landscapers and sign makers, not by climbing groups, so guidebook income is passed on to where it can pay for that work: councils, Rock Climbing Queensland and theCrag.

sections.linkLabel: How KAYA works with local climbing organisations

items.question: Do I have to pay to use the guides?
items.answer: Full guidebook access comes with a KAYA subscription. Prices change, so check KAYA for the current ones. Part of what KAYA earns goes to the guide's author, and at least 5% goes to the local climbing organisation.

items.question: Is this replacing the printed guides?
items.answer: No. The people who wrote the existing guides did the hard yards, and we're grateful for it. The trouble is that nothing current and easy to keep up to date exists for a lot of South East Queensland, so that's what we're building.

items.question: Which South East Queensland guides are on KAYA?
items.answer: We're working on the first ones now. Each crag's progress is on the crag map, and we'll list every guide here as it goes live.

items.question: Does KAYA work for climbing gyms too?
items.answer: Yes, KAYA also has tools for indoor gyms and route setters. See kayaclimb.com/forgyms for the details.
